title: Slim adaptor: declarative operators and compact streaming handshake (PRD sketch)
body:
Executive summary:

This sketch proposes a minimal, declarative SDK surface for Hosted API clients that exposes a small set of 'operators' (declarative intents) rather than explicit tool call plumbing. The runtime and the SDK collaborate during the streaming handshake to decide whether to: (a) perform a remote tool call, (b) respond locally via a compact adaptor (toolless handoff), or (c) synthesize structured output directly in-stream. Goal is to reduce integration friction for product teams, shrink client-side boilerplate, and allow the Hosted runtime to make cost/latency tradeoffs dynamically while preserving strong structured-output contracts.

Why this is needed (problem):
- Integrations often need three things at once: low-latency partial responses, reliable structured output (JSON-like), and optional tool invocation. Current SDKs force engineers to either implement full tool plumbing (complex) or use blunt callbacks that lose structure and observability.
- Many common tool interactions are lightweight (lookup, formatting, deterministic enrichment) and can be handled by small adaptors rather than full remote tool RPCs. But there is no standard place to declare them or fallback from remote->local.
- Streaming and partial responses today are token-focused; developers want declarative contracts that describe intent (e.g., extract-field, fetch-entity, format-table) so the platform can choose the most efficient execution path.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Shipping a slim SDK surface that is trivial to adopt in 30 minutes for common use-cases (summaries, extraction, enrichment).
- Reduce median perceived latency for tool-like interactions by enabling in-client adaptors and prefetch opportunities.
- Ensure structured output contracts (schema enforcement) are maintained end-to-end with telemetry.
- Give runtime the ability to downgrade remote tool calls to local adaptors automatically when safe (graceful degradation).

Non-goals:
- Replace full-fledged tool orchestration for complex workflows (long-running jobs, secure external APIs). We still expect customers to define explicit tool connectors where security/authorization is required.
- Solve every SDK language/platform ergonomics problem in this PRD — we target JS/TS + Python initial surfaces.

Design overview (high level):
1) Declarative operator model: SDK exposes a small enum-like set of operators with typed inputs and outputs. Examples: extract_fields, canonicalize_name, lookup_entity, render_table, invoke_tool_external. Operators are intentionally coarse-grained so adoption is easy.

2) Operator declaration in prompt/metadata: Client can declare a set of desired operators when opening a session or making a call. Declaration includes optional lightweight schema (JSON Schema subset) for expected output.

3) Compact streaming handshake: During session initiation, the client and runtime exchange capability manifests. The manifest indicates what operators the client can locally satisfy (adaptor present), platform preferences (latency-first, cost-first), and whether tool calls require explicit authorization. The runtime responds with an execution plan hint (local-first / remote-first / hybrid).

4) Toolless handoff (local adaptors): If an operator is declared and a client adaptor is available, the runtime may emit a structured operator event into the stream (compact frame) rather than performing a remote tool RPC. SDK adaptors consume those frames and return a typed result back into the session, enabling sub-50ms enrichments when network+compute allow.

5) Structured output commits: Model-generated structured outputs are emitted as typed frames with schema metadata. The SDK validates and commits or rejects frames according to the declared schema and optional 'relaxation' policy (strict | best_effort). Rejected frames surface a validation event so the model can reattempt in the same session.

API / SDK ergonomics (sketch):
- JS example:
  const session = Redwood.hosted.session({operators: ['extract_fields','render_table'], schema: { /* json schema */ }, prefs: {latency: 'low'}})
  session.on('operator', async op => { /* sdk adaptor handles op if local */ })
  const stream = await session.stream(prompt)
  for await (const frame of stream) { switch(frame.type) { case 'text': ...; case 'operator_event': /* structured event */ } }

- Python: similar pattern with async iterator and small adaptor interface (handle_operator(op_name, payload) -> result).

Streaming frames (compact framing):
- Frames are deliberately small and typed: text_chunk, operator_event, structured_commit, validation_error, checkpoint.
- operator_event includes: operator_name, id, input_payload (typed), required_by (optional: token index), expected_schema_ref.
- structured_commit includes: id, schema_ref, payload, confidence, source (model|adaptor|tool).

Fallback and routing policy:
- Execution hints allow runtime to prefer remote tools when adaptor missing or when policy mandates (e.g., authorized data).
- If an adaptor fails or returns null, runtime can fall back to remote tool call automatically per client prefs. This fallback should be observable in telemetry.

Observability and safety:
- All operator events and structured commits are logged with token-level latencies, adaptor id, and resolution path (local/remote).
- Schema violations produce a validation_error frame and an optional model retry.

Security and privacy considerations:
- To enable toolless handoffs, adaptors run in client context and must be explicitly registered in the session manifest; sensitive operators (e.g., access_secrets) are never eligible for local adaptors.
- Authorization: remote tool calls remain gated by explicit OAuth/KMS flows; runtime will advertise auth requirements in the handshake.

Migration and compatibility notes:
- The new surface is additive. Existing SDK callers that do not declare operators see unchanged behavior.
- Provide a shim for older SDKs where operator frames appear as a generic tool_callback event to preserve forward compatibility.

Developer and product workflows this unlocks:
- Mobile clients that need low-latency entity lookups can implement a small JSON adaptor and avoid round-trips for 70% of lookups.
- Embeds and chatbots can require a strict structured_commit schema to prevent hallucinated JSON in production.
- Platform can automatically recommend quantized model variants for sessions declared 'latency-first' to hit SLOs while using toolless handoffs to reduce cost.

Open questions (short list):
- Operators: how many to start with? Recommendation: start with 6 (extraction, normalization, lookup, render_table, format_text, external_invoke).
- Schema references: should we use stable schema ids in the model catalog or allow ad-hoc inline schemas? Hybrid approach suggested: encourage catalog ids but allow inline for dev speed.
- Telemetry volume: operator events increase telemetry. Need sampling rules and retention policy.
- SDK language parity: JS/TS first, then Python. Native mobile SDKs later—what surface parity is required?

Implementation roadmap (next steps):
- Spike (2 weeks): implement handshake + compact framing in hosted runtime + simple JS adaptor that responds to extract_fields with local rules. Create demo mobile web app. (owner: Jordan)
- Spec (1 week): finalize operator enum and minimal JSON Schema subset. (owner: Priya)
- Integrations (3 sprints): ship JS SDK changes, observability hooks, and runtime routing policy. Early adopter program with 2 customer integrations. (owners: product + solutions)

Acceptance criteria (for initial beta):
- SDK can declare operators and receive operator_event frames during streaming sessions.
- Local adaptor path completes >50% of declared operator events in demo app with median latency <60ms.
- Structured_commit frames validate against declared schema; invalid commits produce validation_error frames and surface for model retry.
- Telemetry surface exists mapping operator_event -> resolution path -> latency -> cost estimate.

Notes / links:
- See INF-4123 for initial runtime handshake prototype (Jira).
- Prototype adaptor and minimal demo at github.com/redwood-inference/hosted-sdk (PR #678).

Notes to self (TODOs):
- Get SRE input on sampling and retention for operator telemetry.
- Align schema registry plan with model catalog team.
- Draft developer migration guide and example notebook.

This is intentionally a thin-sketch meant to capture the core idea (declarative operators + compact streaming handshake + toolless handoffs). Goal: get a small, iterative beta in front of a couple of teams to validate latency/cost tradeoffs before widening operator set.
summary_notes: Thin PRD sketch proposing declarative operator model + compact streaming frames to enable local adaptors and improve latency/structured-output guarantees. Targets JS/TS + Python beta.
